title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools designed to help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch if they need more control over their data or a cost-effective solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid tool with a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Plane requires more technical expertise to set up, while Jira offers a more straightforward onboarding process.
* Scalability: Jira is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams.
* Integration difference: Jira has a wider range of integrations with third-party tools, while Plane has a more limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Scalable and suitable for large teams
* User-friendly interface
* Robust project management features
* Limited control over data ownership
**Plane:**
* Free and self-hosted
* Full control over data ownership
* Customizable and flexible
* Suitable for smaller to medium-sized teams
* Limited integrations with third-party tools

## When to Choose Each
Jira is the better choice for large teams with complex projects that require a wide range of integrations and a scalable solution. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize a user-friendly interface and robust project management features. On the other hand, Plane is the better choice for smaller to medium-sized teams that value data ownership and a cost-effective solution. It is also suitable for teams with technical expertise that can handle the setup and customization of the tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane instance on your server.
3. Use the Plane import tool to migrate your data from Jira.
4. Configure your Plane instance to match your team's workflow and needs.
5. Test your Plane instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited integrations and technical requirements. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane requires a high level of technical expertise to set up and customize. However, for teams that value data ownership and a cost-effective solution, Plane is a viable alternative to Jira, and we recommend switching if you have a small to medium-sized team with simple project management needs.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced project management features
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and control
* Teams with technical expertise that can handle the setup and customization of Plane
* Teams that do not require a wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Teams that are looking for a cost-effective solution

## FAQ
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted, which means you can host it on your own server without paying any licensing fees.
### Does Plane have a user-friendly interface?
No, Plane has a more technical interface that requires a higher level of expertise to set up and customize.
### Can I integrate Plane with third-party tools?
Yes, but Plane has a limited set of integrations compared to Jira, so you may need to develop custom integrations for your specific use case.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is better suited for smaller to medium-sized teams due to its technical requirements and limited scalability.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: WeKan is a free, self-hosted alternative to Trello. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Zoom vs Jitsi Meet
comparison_markdown:
# Zoom vs Jitsi Meet (2026)

## Overview
Zoom and Jitsi Meet are video conferencing tools that enable teams to collaborate remotely. This comparison is useful for teams looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted solution, with a core use case of secure and customizable video meetings. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Zoom offers a free plan with limited features, while Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Jitsi Meet allows users to self-host their meetings, giving them full control over their data, while Zoom stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Jitsi Meet requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while Zoom has a more user-friendly interface.
* Scalability: Zoom is designed to handle large-scale meetings and has more robust infrastructure, while Jitsi Meet can be more resource-intensive and may require more servers to scale.
* Feature difference: Zoom has a more polished and feature-rich mobile app, while Jitsi Meet has better support for browser-based meetings and screen sharing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Zoom | Jitsi Meet |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $13.33+/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $666.50/month (50 x $13.33) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2,666/month (200 x $13.33) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Zoom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Robust infrastructure for large-scale meetings
* Feature-rich mobile app
* Integrates with many third-party tools
* Limited control over data storage and security
**Jitsi Meet:**
* Completely free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Browser-based meetings and screen sharing
* Customizable and extensible
* Steeper learning curve for setup and configuration
* Limited mobile app support

## When to Choose Each
Zoom is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have large-scale meeting requirements. It's ideal for teams with limited technical expertise and those who need a polished mobile app experience. On the other hand, Jitsi Meet is suitable for teams that value data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring the platform. It's ideal for small to medium-sized teams with technical expertise and those who prioritize browser-based meetings and screen sharing.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Zoom meeting data in CSV format using the Zoom API or web interface.
2. Set up a Jitsi Meet server using a cloud provider or self-hosting on your own infrastructure.
3. Import your meeting data into Jitsi Meet using the Jitsi Meet API or a third-party import tool.
4. Configure your Jitsi Meet settings and customize the platform to your needs.
5. Test your Jitsi Meet setup and ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Jitsi Meet is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and configure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Jitsi Meet can be resource-intensive and may require more servers to scale. However, for teams that value data control and customization, Jitsi Meet is a viable alternative to Zoom, and we recommend switching if you have the technical expertise and resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need a mobile app
* Technical teams that value data control and customization
* Teams with limited budget and no need for large-scale meetings
* Educational institutions that prioritize open-source solutions
* Non-profit organizations that require self-hosting for security and compliance

## FAQ
### Is Jitsi Meet completely free?
Yes, Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source, with no costs per user or meeting.
### Can I self-host Jitsi Meet?
Yes, Jitsi Meet can be self-hosted on your own infrastructure, giving you full control over your data.
### Does Jitsi Meet have a mobile app?
Jitsi Meet has limited mobile app support, but it's not as polished as Zoom's mobile app.
### Can I import my Zoom meeting data into Jitsi Meet?
Yes, you can import your Zoom meeting data into Jitsi Meet using the Jitsi Meet API or a third-party import tool.
### Is Jitsi Meet suitable for large-scale meetings?
Jitsi Meet can be resource-intensive and may require more servers to scale, so it's not ideal for large-scale meetings.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two popular database management tools used for organizing and tracking data. Both tools offer a range of features that benefit individuals, teams, and businesses, but the key reason someone would switch from Airtable to NocoDB is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and scalable database solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan with limited features, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted, eliminating per-user costs.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Airtable stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Both tools are scalable, but NocoDB's self-hosted nature allows for more flexibility in terms of customization and scaling.
* Feature difference: Airtable has a more comprehensive set of integrations with third-party apps, while NocoDB offers more advanced data modeling capabilities.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Airtable
* User-friendly interface
* Comprehensive set of integrations with third-party apps
* Scalable and reliable
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Limited control over data ownership and storage
### NocoDB
* Self-hosted and free
* Advanced data modeling capabilities
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Offers full control over data ownership and storage
* Requires technical expertise to set up and manage
* Limited integrations with third-party apps

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for teams and businesses that prioritize ease of use and a comprehensive set of integrations with third-party apps. It is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that do not require advanced data modeling capabilities and are willing to pay for a scalable and reliable solution. On the other hand, NocoDB is a good choice for teams and businesses that require full control over their data and storage, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing a self-hosted solution. It is suitable for larger teams or enterprises that require advanced data modeling capabilities and customization.

4. Configure and customize the NocoDB instance to meet specific needs.
5. Test and verify that all data has been successfully migrated.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and polish compared to Airtable. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that NocoDB's integration with third-party apps is still limited. However, for teams and businesses that require full control over their data and storage, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing a self-hosted solution, NocoDB is a clear choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that do not require advanced integrations with third-party apps and want to reduce costs.
* Medium-sized teams that require advanced data modeling capabilities and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and managing a self-hosted solution.
* Large enterprises that require full control over their data and storage and have the technical expertise to set up and manage a self-hosted solution.
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and security.
* Businesses that are looking for a highly customizable and scalable solution.
